newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to build T$47.2 bln port near Keelung.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to build T$47.2 bln port near Keelung.

text.p: Taiwan's transport ministry said on Wednesday it had approved a 13-year, T$47.2 billion project to build a new port adjacent to the island's crowded northern port of Keelung.
"The new port project will increase Keelung's overall capacities," a ministry official told Reuters by telephone.

The ministry envisages the project as a public-private partnership, proposing to build seven docks and facilities with private firms contributing T$21.8 billion of the total T$47.2 billion project, the official said.
Private interests will be invited to submit bids to build and operate the port, the official said.
Officials declined to comment further on the project as details require further planning by Keelung port.
The ministry approved the plan on Tuesday, officials said.
Keelung port, a natural harbour, is the main container and grain facility in northern Taiwan. Its three container terminals can handle 14 20,000-tonne class ships at once.

The port handled 25.4 million tonnes of trade in 1994 and has been planning an expansion for years, partly reflecting an expected rise in throughput if Keelung, like Kaohsiung in the south, begins transshipping cargoes to and from mainland China.

Taiwan business interests are keen to increase the island's role in the development of mainland China's economy, despite a bitter rivalry that has split Taiwan and China on ideological lines since a civil war divided them in 1949.
Taiwan's Nationalist government still bans direct links with the communist mainland and is wary of allowing Taiwan to become overdependent on its adversary's economy.
Although Taipei has allowed local and mainland ships to sail directly between Kaohsiung and two nearby mainland ports since April, it still forbids mainland cargoes from entering Taiwan's customs.
Likewise, Taiwan cargoes cannot be loaded for direct passage to the mainland.
Keelung can now handle ships of up to 30,000 tonnes. It was not immediately known if the expansion would enable it to handle larger vessels.

Local media reported the port development would be based on the build-operate-transfer model -- enabling private firms to build and operate the port for decades before transferring operating rights to the government after maybe 50 years.
